If you bring the science and want to build something impactful with an ambitious, creative team, join us!
summary: LunaRim answers the two questions every lunar south pole mission faces: where to land, and when. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hangs low, so a ridge a few kilometres away decides whether a lander has power and a direct radio link. LunaRim combines NASA LOLA terrain (a horizon for each of 290,364 grid points, out to 200 km) with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions for every hour from 2026 to 2045, and scores each site and landing hour from 0 to 100 against mission rules such as light days, the longest night the battery must survive, Earth visibility and slope (defaults based on NASA's 2024 lander requirements). Three views share the same data and rules: pick a landing window and see the best sites on a map, pick a site and get its best dates, or explore every site that has a valid landing window in the coming years. When a launch slips, a new best date comes back in seconds. LunaRim runs offline on a laptop and helps mission planners, educators and the public compare scenarios quickly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunaRim is a web app for choosing a landing site and date at the lunar south pole (80–90° S). For every 1 km grid point and every hour from 2026 to 2045 it evaluates sunlight for power and Earth visibility for direct-to-Earth communication against the real terrain horizon. Three views share one data set and one rulebook:

- Time selection: pick a landing window; a map scores every site for each landing hour, with a time slider, the five best sites and data layers.

- Site selection: pick a site (map, coordinates or known sites such as Malapert or Connecting Ridge); LunaRim searches every hour for the best landing dates and alternatives.

- Explore sites: see every site that has at least one valid landing window in the coming years, with a ranking.

For any site, LunaRim shows the horizon profile with 30-day Sun and Earth tracks, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, light days, the longest night compared with battery capacity, mean illumination, Earth visibility, the longest radio gap, Earth visibility during the mission, a score breakdown, and whether an excluded site is a near miss or clearly excluded.

HOW IT WORKS

- Terrain: NASA LOLA south pole elevation models (80 m near field, 240 m far field) give a horizon mask for 290,364 grid points, in 720 directions out to 200 km, for a 2 m mast.

- Sky: JPL Horizons (DE441) sub-solar and sub-Earth points every hour from 2026 to 2045, including libration; Earth elevation corrected for topocentric parallax.

- Scoring: all points are evaluated with vectorised NumPy code. The score combines a Sun score (light days, longest darkness, mean illumination), an Earth score (visibility, longest radio gap, contact after landing), simultaneous Sun and Earth visibility, slope (steepest value inside the landing ellipse) and optional proximity to permanently shadowed regions. Hard exclusions: landing region (crewed: within 6° of the pole), slope over 10°, too few light days for mission plus buffer, a night during the mission longer than the battery lasts (50 h), Earth visible less than 25 % of the time, and an optional minimum for Earth visibility during the mission. Automated tests compare the vectorised results point by point with the reference implementation.

- Runs offline from a 138 MB data extract in the repository; a data panel can re-download LOLA, re-query Horizons and recompute horizons.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

LunaRim turns ephemeris tables and elevation models into a clear verdict in seconds, so teams can re-plan when hardware delays move a launch. It explains why a site fails, which makes it useful for teaching as well as planning. Example with the default crewed rules: 10,023 of 290,364 sites have at least one valid landing window between November 2026 and November 2029; the best lies near the Malapert massif, an Artemis III candidate region, with a best date of 7 October 2027.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python 3 (standard-library web server), NumPy, SciPy, optional rasterio for LOLA GeoTIFFs; JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet 1.9.4; no build step and no cloud services; Git and GitHub. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with coding, testing, debugging and documentation.

CREATIVITY

LunaRim answers both "where" and "when" with the same rules, separates near misses from clear exclusions, and draws the Sun and Earth paths over the real skyline so users can see which ridge blocks them.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

No atmosphere, so the horizon is purely geometric; the Sun counts as lit when at least half its disc is visible; terrain out to 200 km; worst-case slope inside the landing ellipse (IM-1 and IM-2 both tipped over); battery checked only against nights during the mission; libration and parallax; stated limits (1 km grid, horizons stored to 0.01°, coarse shadow estimate); accessibility (high-contrast theme, colour-blind-safe Viridis and Okabe–Ito palettes, keyboard control); runs offline on an ordinary laptop.
